newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS -- France trims interest rates after EMU deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -- France trims interest rates after EMU deal.

text.p: The Bank of France trimmed two key interest rates on Tuesday in a move interpreted by economists as a speedy vote of confidence in last weekend's deal on control of public deficits when the euro single currency is created.

The independent central bank shaved its intervention rate by a tiny five-hundredths of a percent, to 3.15 percent from 3.20 percent. It cut another less crucial one, the five-to-10 rate, to 4.60 percent from 4.75 percent.

The cuts, effective from Thursday coming, were announced after a meeting of the Bank's monetary policy council and took most economists slightly by surprise, even if continued policy of small, gradual cuts in the short term had been expected.

The changes will have little or no beneficial impact on the economy but show the Bank is confident in the "stability pact" struck by European Union leaders at their weekend Dublin summit on deficit control once the "euro" comes into being.

"This is a very good sign the Bank of France is sending us. It's really telling us it's happy with the stability pact, which nobody doubted, but it shows they've resumed easing," said David Naude, economist at U.S. investment bank JP Morgan.
"Some people are saying they will go through German rates, which I do not believe at all, but they will move toward German rates, the question is how fast," he said.
As long as people don't believe that this is the start of a devaluation, which I don't believe for a moment, it could have a positive effect on markets," Naude added.

Jean-Louis Mourier, economist at Louis Dreyfus Finance, said the move was a positive sign and, like Naude, said he believed the cut was motivated by the "stabilty pact" rather than recent calls from two monetary policy council members for speedier cuts in rates.
Those calls came from monetary policy council members Paul Marcehlli and Jean-Pierre Gerard, seen as a minority in the nine-member council keen on a less stringent monetary policy.
"It's a surprise all the same. I think the objective is to close in on German rates but I do not think this is a victory for the thesis of Marchelli and Gerard," Mourier said.
